subcategory: New Zealand native bushfood and medicinal shrub

planting.note: Set out nursery-grown rooted cuttings once the frost-free season has arrived and soil has warmed; young plants need overhead shelter from hard frost until established.

directions: Plant this heart-leaved New Zealand forest shrub in dappled shade with consistently moist, free-draining soil, since it naturally grows in the understory of coastal and lowland bush. The glossy, often moth-perforated leaves are the part most often harvested, dried, and steeped for a peppery herbal tea, while the small orange fruiting spikes are edible once fully ripe. Expect a rooted cutting to bulk up into a useful harvestable shrub within one to two years, but shelter young plants from cold wind and hard frost for their first few winters, since mature specimens tolerate only light, brief frost. Trim lightly after flowering to keep growth bushy and encourage fresh leaf production.
sources: Te Ara — The Encyclopedia of New Zealand

subcategory: New Zealand native tree with edible fruit aril and traditional seed oil

planting.note: Remove the fleshy aril before sowing fresh seed, since viability drops quickly; grow seedlings under cover and transplant out once the trunk has hardened, protecting young trees through their first several winters.

directions: This handsome evergreen tree from New Zealand's lowland forests produces clusters of black seeds wrapped in a bright orange, fleshy aril that is sweet and edible straight off the tree, unlike the hard seed itself. Traditionally the oily seeds were roasted and pressed to yield titoki oil, used by Maori as a skin and hair treatment and for dressing wounds. Allow five to ten years for a young tree to reach fruiting size, and give it a sheltered, sunny to lightly shaded site, since the pinnate glossy foliage and shallow root flare can be damaged by strong wind exposure. Young trees need frost protection for their first few winters, but established titoki tolerate coastal conditions and occasional light frost well.
sources: Te Ara — The Encyclopedia of New Zealand

subcategory: New Zealand native coastal tree; fruit flesh edible, kernel requires traditional processing to remove toxin

planting.note: Sow fresh seed with the orange flesh removed; grow on in containers and plant out to a sheltered, frost-protected site once well rooted, since young trees are sensitive to cold.

directions: Karaka is a glossy-leaved coastal forest tree bearing orange, plum-like fruit with a sweet edible outer flesh, but the large kernel inside is naturally toxic and was only ever consumed after an elaborate traditional process of steaming or boiling followed by days of soaking or burying to leach out the karakin toxin, after which it became an important staple starch for Maori communities. Grow it in a sheltered, full-sun to lightly shaded coastal or lowland position with reasonable drainage, allowing roughly five to ten years before a young tree reaches fruiting size. Protect seedlings from hard frost and strong wind while establishing, since mature specimens handle salt-laden coastal air well. Never attempt to eat the raw kernel or an untreated fruit in quantity, since both the seed and unprocessed flesh remain unsafe without proper preparation.
sources: Te Ara — The Encyclopedia of New Zealand

planting.note: Plant rooted slips after the last frost once soil has warmed well above 60°F; mound soil into ridges to encourage tuber formation in this smaller-rooted heritage line.

directions: Owairaka Red is one of the few pre-European kumara lines still maintained today by New Zealand heritage seed-savers, descended from cultivars grown by Maori communities long before larger, higher-yielding modern cultivars became dominant. Its tubers are smaller and less prolific than commercial sweet potatoes but are valued for distinctive flavor and cultural history, with deep reddish-purple skin over pale flesh. Plant slips in warm, light, well-drained soil in full sun once all frost danger has passed, mounding the rows to give the modest root system room to swell. Harvest before the first autumn frost, since the vines and tubers have no cold tolerance at all.
sources: Koanga Institute (New Zealand heritage seed library)

planting.note: Start seed indoors well ahead of the last frost, since germination is slow and erratic, then transplant into hot, free-draining, sandy soil once nights stay reliably warm.

directions: Bush tomato is a low, spreading desert subshrub from Central Australia whose small fruit ripen and naturally dry on the plant into a wrinkled, raisin-like state, which is how Aboriginal communities have long harvested and stored it as kutjera, or desert raisin. It needs hot, sunny, sharply drained sandy soil and minimal watering once established, since overwatering in humid climates invites root rot in this true arid-zone native. Treat it as a heat-loving annual or short-lived perennial outside true desert climates, starting seed indoors well ahead of the last frost and setting plants out only once soil is thoroughly warm. The dried fruit has a strong, slightly bitter, caramel-like flavor and is ground into the bush tomato seasoning now sold commercially across Australia.
sources: Australian National Botanic Gardens plant profile

subcategory: Australian coastal succulent groundcover with edible fruit and leaves

planting.note: Press rooted stem cuttings into sandy, sharply drained soil once frost danger has passed; this succulent roots readily from sections of trailing stem.

directions: Native pigface is a sprawling, salt-tolerant succulent groundcover from Australian coastal dunes and clifftops, most easily grown from stem cuttings pressed into sandy, free-draining soil in full sun. Its thick, finger-like leaves and the ripe, fig-flavored fruit that follows the daisy-like purple-pink flowers are both edible, with the fruit traditionally eaten fresh or made into jam. Expect flowering and fruit within the first one to two years as a cutting knits into a dense mat, after which established plantings tolerate drought, salt spray, and poor sandy soil with almost no supplemental water. Protect young plantings from hard frost until they have filled in, since a mature, interlocking mat is considerably more cold-hardy than a single rooted cutting.
sources: Australian National Botanic Gardens plant profile

subcategory: Central Australian desert wattle grown for edible seed (wattleseed spice)

planting.note: Nick or soak the hard seed coat in near-boiling water to break dormancy before sowing in free-draining potting mix; transplant out once frost danger has passed, since this fast-growing wattle resents later root disturbance.

directions: Acacia colei is a fast-growing, multi-stemmed arid-zone wattle from Central Australia, cultivated specifically for its abundant, protein-rich seed pods, which are roasted and ground into the nutty, coffee-like wattleseed flour used in breads, ice cream, and other bushfood products. It thrives in hot, full sun with poor, sharply drained soil and needs very little water once established, since it is adapted to true desert rainfall and will rot in humid, wet-footed conditions. Scarify or hot-water-treat the hard seed coat before sowing for reliable germination, and expect two to four years of growth before the tree produces pods worth a substantial seed harvest. Established plants tolerate light frost, but young seedlings need protection through their first winter.
sources: Australian National Botanic Gardens plant profile
